newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Economic headaches seen muting Austria's EU cheer.
newsitem.headline: Economic headaches seen muting Austria's EU cheer.

text.p: Austria's economic problems appear legion 22 months after joining the European Union (EU) -- unemployment is rising, insolvencies are running at record levels and exporters are struggling to make ends meet.

With just three days to go until the country's first European Parliament elections, voters look set to blame it all on Brussels, with recent surveys showing 57 percent of Austrians seeing the EU as the main cause of their headaches.
Economists disagree and say the government has not done enough to adequately explain the benefits of membership.
They insist joining Europe's economic bloc had simply helped expose Austria's deep-seated problems of poor competitiveness, a stifling bureaucracy and lavish government spending.
"These issues are all home-grown. EU membership has just made it much more pressing to find solutions," Georg Busch, senior economist at research institute Wifo told Reuters.
But discontent among workers is rife, and reforms are hard to push through in Austria's cosy system of social partnership.

Workers at the southern Austrian tyre plant Semperit last week vowed to block plans by its German parent Continental to move production across the border to the Czech Republic in a bid to avoid Austria's exorbitant wage costs.
Not even Chancellor Franz Vranitzky succeeded in convincing Continental to halt its drive to cut Semperit's 2,400-strong workforce in half by the end of next year.

The sale of Austria's biggest retail chain Billa to German supermarket giant Rewe did little to cheer up the country's grumbling unions, still dreaming of the good old days when industrial strategy was quietly decided between employers and worker representatives over a beer or two.
Foreign firms are not the only ones shedding jobs. Domestic heavyweights such as national grid Verbund or high-grade steel maker Boehler Uddeholm also have announced job cuts.

The reason is not so much the EU as the need to adjust to a sluggish economy at home and across the continent, a slowdown exacerbated by huge cuts in government spending in order to qualify for Europe's planned currency union.
Research insitute Wifo expects Austria's economic growth to slow to 0.7 percent this year, from 1.8 percent in 1995, and unemployment to rise to 7.1 percent from 6.6 percent.
But analysts are quick to point that without the EU, Austria would face an even tougher economic struggle.

"The problem of rising job losses would be even bigger if we hadn't joined the union," Busch said. "And the growth in exports last year, immediately after EU membership, of about 8.5 percent was much bigger than in comparable countries."

Foreign investment shows a similar pattern. Net investment in Austria rose to 16.7 billion schillings ($1.55 billion) in the first half of this year alone, more than triple the sum recorded for all of 1995. It outstripped the 15 billion schillings Austria paid in net dues to the EU's coffers.
"Maybe the advantages of EU membership aren't all that clear to most people. What we really need is for the government to explain it properly," Busch said. ($1=10.76 Schilling)
